html:
The Huna invasions were attacks on north India by the Alchon Huns, a people of Central Asia related to the Hephthalites, from about 455 to about 528 CE. They helped bring down the Gupta Empire.

The first wave came about 455. The Gupta prince Skandagupta beat it back and boasted of the win on a pillar at Bhitari, but the cost emptied his treasury and Gupta gold coins grew poorer.

A second wave succeeded. About 500 the Huna king Toramana took Punjab and pushed as far as Malwa in central India. His son Mihirakula ruled from Sagala, today's Sialkot. Buddhist writers, among them the pilgrim Xuanzang, remember him as a cruel man who destroyed monasteries across Gandhara.

Indian kings joined against him. Yashodharman of Malwa defeated Mihirakula about 528 and set up victory pillars at Mandsaur. Mihirakula withdrew to Kashmir and died soon after.

The damage stayed. The Guptas shrank to a small kingdom and ended about 550. Trade through the northwest fell, the cities and monasteries of Gandhara did not recover, and north India split into rival kingdoms until Harsha.
sum: The Huna invasions were attacks on north India by the Alchon Huns, a people of Central Asia related to the Hephthalites, from about 455 to about 528 CE. They helped bring down the Gupta Empire.
